summary: This RFC defines how to implement channel bindings for EAP methods, to address the lying NAS problem and the lying provider problem, in which a network access server or provider misrepresents who it is or what it offers.

eli5.summary: It lets you check that the one asking for your password is who they claim to be, so a trickster cannot say they are someone else.

questions: how to prevent a lying nas in eap
what is the lying nas problem
how does eap detect a lying provider
what is the eap lower layer radius attribute
subtitle: How an EAP peer and server catch an access point or visited network that lies about what it offers.

tldr.problem: In EAP pass-through mode, the authenticator can tell the peer one thing about the network and the AAA server another, so a less trusted network can pose as a more trusted one or a roaming provider can advertise false terms.
tldr.mechanism: After keys are derived, the peer sends what the authenticator told it (i1) to the EAP server inside an integrity-protected EAP method channel. The server compares i1 with the AAA attributes it received (i2) and a local database, and returns a success or failure code.
tldr.outcome: This catches inconsistencies but cannot say which entity is lying, and it needs updated EAP methods and peer drivers plus a trustworthy database. It is only part of a full defense, since lower layers and EAP methods must still define what to carry.

today: RFC 6677 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says it is only part of a defense: lower layers must still specify what goes in i1 and EAP methods must describe how the data is carried.

sections.title: The Lying NAS and Lying Provider Problems
sections.content:
In the Extensible Authentication Protocol (RFC 3748) pass-through mode, a Network Access Server (NAS), or pass-through authenticator, may give the backend AAA infrastructure one set of facts about itself and give the EAP peer contrary ones. It might even give the same false facts to both. A lying entity can also sit anywhere on the AAA path between the NAS and the EAP server.

The problem arises when the same credentials give access to services that differ in some important way. The RFC's example is an organization with two IEEE 802.11 networks, one low-security for the web and one with confidential information. An access point on the web network could broadcast the SSID of the confidential network in its beacons to lure clients. In roaming, the same trick is the lying provider problem: a visited network advertises attractive rates, and may also see traffic it would not otherwise see.

The solution is EAP channel binding: the peer tells the AAA server, inside the EAP method, what the authenticator told it, and the server checks it.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle can tell you one story and your bank a different one. Channel binding lets you and your bank compare stories privately.

sections.title: Problem Statement and Example Attacks
sections.content:
EAP peers and servers mutually authenticate and derive keys, but the server can be far from the authenticator, with many entities to trust in between. A malicious authenticator, or a compromised proxy relaying false data to it, can misrepresent the network. The goal is to make sure the authenticator gives correct information during discovery, selection and authentication.

The RFC separates enterprise networks, where a single administrative domain can let the server know all authenticators, from service provider networks, where roaming makes global knowledge infeasible and the aim is service consistent with the contract between providers. Its example attacks include:

  • A compromised access point on a guest VLAN advertising the SSID of the corporate network.
  • An EAP GSS-API service, such as an instant messaging server, impersonating a more trusted mail server.
  • A mobile provider advertising flat rates but sending per-minute rates to the home server, or boosting tower power near a border to attract roamers.

The text notes that channel binding can detect inconsistencies but cannot determine which entity is lying.
sections.eli5: A guest-room Wi-Fi might put up the sign of the secret clubhouse. People who think they are safe might share secrets there.

sections.title: How Channel Binding Differs and Where It Runs
sections.content:
EAP channel bindings authenticate information the authenticator advertised to the peer, by letting the peer and server compare their views of network properties over a secure channel. The RFC points out that this differs from the channel bindings of RFC 5056, which bind the endpoints of a multi-layer protocol; the same term was adopted independently for both.

Two approaches are described. The peer and server can exchange plaintext information inside an integrity-protected channel, or both can encode their view into an opaque blob that feeds the session key derivation. This document uses the plaintext approach, which allows policy-based comparison rather than exact matches, is easier to add to methods with extensible protected channels, and allows debugging and a logging-only mode.

Alternatively, a future document could carry bindings in the lower layer's secure association protocol. That would leave EAP methods unchanged but would need a new AAA exchange and an upgrade of every NAS. The scope also varies: in an enterprise the server can verify specific properties such as a MAC address, while in a service provider network it generally can verify only broader facts, such as the network name from roaming agreements.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to compare notes: say the story out loud and check it, or mix the story into your secret handshake so a wrong story makes the handshake fail. This RFC picks saying it out loud.

sections.title: The Channel-Binding Process
sections.content:
The process involves three pieces of information. i1 is the unauthenticated information the authenticator presents to the peer, such as the network identity and offered services. i2 is the AAA attributes the authenticator, or the last hop in the AAA proxy chain, presents to the AAA server. A local database holds trustworthy data about authenticators or roaming partners, and may use wildcards, for example to check that access points on a subnet all use one SSID.

During an EAP method with channel bindings, the peer sends i1 to the EAP server. The server checks the consistency of i1, i2 and the database, then tells the peer whether the check succeeded or failed, and lists the attributes it used. Checking i1 against i2 alone is not enough, because an authenticator could lie consistently to both.

If conformance is mandatory and a check fails, after sending a protected failure indication the EAP server MUST send an EAP-Failure. Otherwise it MUST let the session complete and leave the access decision to the peer's policy. In that case it MUST NOT list non-compliant information among the attributes used, and SHOULD indicate failure.
sections.eli5: You hear a sign (i1), the bank hears a tag from the helper (i2), and the bank has its own list. If all three agree, you are safe.

sections.title: The Channel-Binding Message Format
sections.content:
Channel-binding data and responses share one format: a one-byte Code, followed by repeated groups of Length (two octets, in network byte order, counting only the NS-Specific data), NSID (one octet naming the namespace) and the namespace-specific data. An NSID MUST NOT appear more than once in a message. NSID 1 is RADIUS, and 255 is reserved for private use.

For RADIUS, each attribute is encoded as a one-octet type, a one-octet length that includes those two octets (minimum 3), and the value. The full attribute value is included.

The peer sends code 1, with the full attributes it wants validated. The server returns code 2 on success, listing the attributes it considered, and code 3 on failure, where it SHOULD include any attributes that were validated. Peers MUST treat unknown codes as failure, and MUST ignore attributes under an unknown NSID or not present in their own data.
sections.eli5: The message is a labeled list: first a number saying what kind of message it is, then labeled boxes of facts. The answer is either a yes list or a no.

sections.title: Transport and Layer Requirements
sections.content:
Channel binding must be carried after keying material is derived and before the peer suffers harm from joining an adversarial network. The transport MUST provide end-to-end integrity protection between peer and server, and SHOULD provide confidentiality. If it cannot, private information MUST NOT be sent in the channel-binding information.

Size matters. In one example with an EAP MTU of 1020 octets, EAP-GPSK and maximal-length identities, only 384 octets remain for channel-binding data, while EAP-TTLS supports fragmentation and can carry much more.

An EAP method carrying the data MUST support integrity-protected data in both directions and MUST exchange it with the AAA subsystem hosting the EAP server. Lower layers MUST support EAP and key-deriving methods, and lower-layer specifications must say what goes in i1. The i1 data MUST include the new EAP-Lower-Layer RADIUS attribute (type 163, length 6, 32-bit value) unless a layer-specific attribute is included. On the AAA side, the server should validate NAS-Identifier and NAS-Port-Type against its database, and may check the subnet of NAS-IP-Address and NAS-IPv6-Address against the last-hop proxy.
sections.eli5: The note to the bank must be sealed so the helper cannot change it, and it has to fit in the envelope.

sections.title: Trust Model and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The model assumes an honest peer and server and a possibly malicious authenticator. The server trusts that the information from the peer is what the peer received, the peer trusts the server's result, and the server trusts its database. An EAP method MUST provide mutual authentication, key derivation with an integrity key unknown to the authenticator, and integrity-protected transmission in both directions. If any trust relationship fails, channel binding cannot be provided.

The RFC also warns of limits. A tunnel terminated at the authenticator can defeat cryptographic binding. A dishonest server that claims success cannot be detected and must be handled by policy. Bid-down attacks are hard to prevent because EAP Success messages are not integrity protected, so an attacker such as the NAS could inject one. On privacy, channel-binding data may reveal identifiers, so it must be encrypted or must not carry private data, and a server that fails on a mismatched username can confirm an authenticator's guess.

Deploying it means updating EAP methods and peer drivers, plus an API between the EAP server and the database. No changes to the pass-through authenticator are required.
sections.eli5: It only works if you and your bank really trust each other and nobody can peek at your whisper. If the bank is also dishonest, it cannot help.
